Hands-free refresh

Task Scheduler runs the collector hidden · the page refreshes itself · you click nothing

Two loops, deliberately separated. Collection — Windows Task Scheduler runs the read-only collector in a hidden window on your interval, talking to Azure with your saved session. Display — switch Live on in this bar and the page re-reads local data.js every 30 seconds, refreshing the moment new numbers land. A browser page can't launch programs on your machine — that boundary is the thing our whole department defends — so the launcher lives where launchers belong: Task Scheduler.

Live is not an off switch. Switching it off stops this page re-reading the file; the scheduled task keeps collecting, because a web page cannot reach Task Scheduler any more than it can launch a program. The switch that actually stops Azure reads is option 8 (pause) in Setup-AutoRefresh.cmd: it leaves the task installed but every run then exits without a single Azure call and without writing anything. Option 9 prints what Task Scheduler actually holds — real interval, last result, and the exact log file the task appends to.

Every 5 min

The fastest honest cadence — matches the Azure portal's own auto-refresh floor. Metrics land 1–3 min behind real time regardless.

Every 15 min RECOMMENDED

Right for steady-state capacity monitoring. Fresh enough to catch a climb toward a ceiling, light on ARM quota.

Hourly / 4-hourly

For quiet fleets. Pair with the metric alert rules from the command reference so spikes page you instead of a poll.

Daily 06:00

The morning briefing: yesterday's peaks and any tier drift, on screen before stand-up.

1Double-click Setup-AutoRefresh.cmd in the WATCHMAN folder 2Pick an interval from the menu 3Switch  Live  on up here — done, forever Need one off-cycle refresh?  Copy update command  puts the exact command for this folder on your clipboard — paste it into a terminal. This page notices the new data and refreshes itself.
Why not every 5 or 30 seconds? Azure Monitor ingests platform metrics on a 1–3 minute delay and throttles aggressive polling (HTTP 429), so sub-minute collection returns identical numbers at real cost. The 30-second cycle lives in the right place: this page checking a local file. Sign-in: scheduled runs reuse your saved Az session; if it ever expires they log a note to the audit file and skip — never a hidden prompt — and one interactive run of Update-Dashboard.cmd restores them. The task runs as you, at least privilege, no admin and no stored password; pause, inspect or remove it any time from the same setup menu. If the interval you picked is not the interval you get: the setup script reads the cadence back out of Task Scheduler after registering and refuses to claim success when the two disagree, so option 9 always shows the truth rather than the label you clicked.

Know the ceiling before you reach it.

Operator notes

    
    
      
  • Alert on these at NIC scope: CurrentTotalFlowsIn
        CurrentTotalFlowsOut CreationRateMaxTotalFlowsIn
        CreationRateMaxTotalFlowsOut. 
    • 
      
  • Tier changes take downtime. Stop/start for standalone VMs; drain one side of an
        active-active pair while the other is updated. The DR hub fix is a change-window item.
    • 
      
  • Management NICs stay unaccelerated by design — the dimmed blue ports are correct
        as-is.
    • 
      
  • Flows and bandwidth are different questions. An SD-WAN edge can carry a handful
        of long-lived tunnels — a near-zero flow count — while moving millions of packets.
        A NIC that looks idle on this panel can be busy in the portal's packet chart, and both are
        right. Read flow pressure here; read bandwidth and packets on the Internet Edge panel and
        the Throughput / Packet-rate views. Capacity (tier) spend follows the flow model above.
    • 
      
  • Tiers bill hourly per NIC. Size to observed peak plus failover math, not
        symmetry.
    •

How every flow number on this page is calculated

    
    
      
  • Statistic: peak, not latest. Each figure is the highest
        CurrentTotalFlows value inside the selected window. Flows are a gauge;
        the peak is what reaches the ceiling and drops packets, and the latest reading hides it.
    • 
      
  • Scope: per interface, never summed. On a forwarding appliance the same
        conversation is counted on the ingress and the egress NIC, so adding interfaces
        double-counts. Each appliance is reported by the interface closest to its own ceiling,
        and that interface is named on the card.
    • 
      
  • Ceiling: the Accelerated Connections tier on that interface.
        A1 = 1M, A2 = 2M, A4 = 4M, A8 = 8M connections. The tier is bought per NIC, so it is the
        only denominator that belongs to the numerator above it.
    • 
      
  • No tier means no measurement. Where Accelerated Connections is off, Azure
        publishes no flow metric at all. Those appliances are marked
        No flow telemetry rather than shown at zero — zero would read as healthy
        when it actually means blind.
    • 
    

    
Fleet Health and the Accelerated Connections panel below call the same functions,
       so they cannot disagree. Cross-check any figure against the appliance itself
       (show session info on the firewall, show security flow session summary
       on Junos) — the platforms count sessions, Azure counts SDN five-tuple flows, so
       compare trends rather than expecting the absolute numbers to match.

    public-facing interface bandwidth — the first place to look when users report slowness


  

    

      
Public interface throughput

      

        
        
      

    

    

    

    

    

      Reading this for latency. Azure reports how much traffic crossed the edge, never how long it took.
      A public interface pinned near its ceiling is a credible cause of user-visible slowness; one sitting at a
      few percent while users complain moves the investigation off bandwidth and onto DNS, routing, the ISP,
      or the application itself. Sustained Tx saturation with flat Rx often means egress backup or replication,
      not user demand.

Application-level visibility lives in the appliance OS, not Azure

    
Azure Monitor sees layer 3/4 — flows, bytes, packets — and cannot name the application inside a flow.
    App-ID on the firewalls can. For per-application top talkers, use the ACC on each firewall or, read-only from the CLI:
    show session all filter count yes · show session info ·
    debug dataplane pool statistics. A future collector extension can pull App-ID top applications
    over the the appliance vendor API and render them here alongside the Azure metrics — say the word when you want that built.

Activity & Audit
every run, every Azure call, every local write — with operator, timestamp and the exact command line · appended by the tooling, never written by this page

  

    

      
Recent activity

      

        
        

          
          
          
          
        

      

    

    

    

      Full transparency, by construction. Every WATCHMAN script writes to
      watchman-activity-YYYY-MM.log before and after it acts: sign-in and context switches,
      each Get-Az* call with its target, every file written, registry and scheduled-task
      changes, sanitized exports, Update-button clicks, and any refusal to write. Lines carry the local
      timestamp with UTC offset, the category, and DOMAIN\user@computer; every run records
      its full command line, so an interactive run, a scheduled run and a button-launched run are
      distinguishable forever. Read it in a terminal with View-Log.cmd
      (-Runs, -Summary, -Category AZURE-READ, -Follow,
      -Csv), or run any collection with -VerboseLog to watch each line as it is
      written. This panel is a convenience copy of the tail — the .log files are the record.
    

  






  

    

      WATCHMAN — Flow-capacity monitoring for Azure network virtual appliances.
      Read-only view of Azure Monitor per-NIC metrics collected by Update-Dashboard.cmd.
      Flow gauges use Maximum aggregation because peaks, not averages, cause packet drops;
      CurrentTotalFlows* is only published on NICs with Accelerated Connections enabled, which is
      why some interfaces show bandwidth but no flows. Azure platform metrics retain 93 days. All times shown are this machine’s local time — never UTC.
